results.title: Intellectual humility: From Ancient Biblical Proverbs to 21st Century Research. - The Soggy Spaniel
results.content: The Soggy Spaniel > pride > Intellectual humility: From Ancient Biblical Proverbs to 21st Century Research. # Intellectual humility: From Ancient Biblical Proverbs to 21st Century Research. The solution is Biblical, and it’s called intellectual humility. Intellectual humility is the honest and willing admission that our knowledge is limited and our reasoning imperfect, with an ability to tolerate disagreement in a calm and respectful manner. According to Robson, highly intelligent people are much more confident, and this confidence makes them less likely to doubt their opinions or change their minds. But it’s difficult to measure intellectual humility in a research setting, and one must be careful to distinguish between intelligence and knowledge. One thing we know for sure is that intelligence does not protect against cognitive biases, although it does tend to correlate with higher curiosity and higher cognitive reflection (“thinking slow” – Kahneman). Recent research has found a consistent correlation between intellectual humility and other principles of sound thinking: having a growth mindset, curiosity, open-minded thinking, cognitive reflection, and emotional regulation. In a 2021 paper, researchers found that intellectual humility partially offsets the Dunning-Kruger effect. A team of researchers from Israel and the UK found that those who rejected vaccination were less inclined to believe well-established facts, more inclined toward “alternative facts”, and scored significantly lower in intellectual humility. Another team of researchers from Texas A&M found a strong correlation between intellectual humility and willingness to be vaccinated – and between lack of humility and anti-vaccination attitudes. In 2021, an international team writing in *Nature Human Behavior* called attention to the replication crisis in social, behavioral, and life sciences – and the need for greater humility and transparency about the limitations of research. results.title: Owning One’s Intellectual Limitations A Review of Intellectual Humility
results.content:
Title: Owning One’s Intellectual Limitations A Review of Intellectual Humility
In recent years, intellectual humility (IH) has become an emerging topic in psychological research. IH has been defined by different psychological researchers as, “insight of the limits of one’s knowledge” (McElroy et al., 2014); “a nonthreatening awareness of one’s intellectual fallibility” (Krumrei-Mancuso & Rouse, 2016); “recognizing that a particular personal belief may be fallible, accompanied by an appropriate attentiveness to limitations in the evidentiary basis of that belief and to one’s own limitations in obtaining and evaluating relevant information” (Leary et al., 2017), et al. Based on the conceptualization of Meagher, Leman, Bias, Latendresse, & Rowatt (2015), Haggard and her associates (2016,2018) developed a 12-item IH scale (e.g., “I am quick to acknowledge my intellectual limitations”), which measures three main components of IH: owning one’s intellectual limitations, appropriate discomfort with intellectual limitations, and love of learning. The general IH scale includes unidimensional 6 items (e.g., “I reconsider my opinions when presented with new evidence”), which is proven not to be contaminated by socially desirable responses (Leary et al., 2017). (2015) adapted the cultural humility scale (Hook et al., 2013) to a 12-item IH scale (e.g., “Thinks he/she understands more than he/she actually does”), including two factors: positive other-oriented characteristics (7 items), and superiority and making assumptions (5 items). (2017) developed a multidimensional scale to measure the four factors of IH: open-mindedness, intellectual modesty, corrigibility, and engagement (e.g., “Being smarter than other people is not especially important to me/him”). Regarding personality, most empirical studies consistently demonstrated that intellectually humble people are high in agreeableness, conscientiousness, openness, and emotional stability, and have a greater need for cognition and curiosity (Davis et al., 2016;Haggard et al., 2018;Hoyle et al., 2016;Krumrei-Mancuso, Haggard, LaBouff, & Rowatt, 2020;McElroy et al., 2014;Meagher et al., 2015;Porter & Schumann, 2018). The research using informant-report measure also showed that the perception of others’ IH is positively related to the perception of that person’s agreeableness, openness, conscientiousness, and emotional stability (McElroy et al., 2014). Research in developmental psychology also showed that children with high intelligence have higher IH after controlling age, and this connection is specific to the cognitive aspect of IH, but not its social aspect (Danovitch et al., 2019).

results.title: Honesty-Humility in the HEXACO Model | Relaza
results.content: # Honesty-Humility in the HEXACO Model. In the HEXACO model, **Honesty-Humility** is one of the six main traits that characterize individual differences in moral and social aspects of human behavior. This characteristic reflects a tendency towards honesty, conscientiousness, and humility in relation to oneself and others. ## Definition of Honesty-Humility. Honesty-Humility in the HEXACO model is a measure of a person's inclination towards honest and fair behavior. People with high levels of this trait exhibit conscientiousness, avoid manipulation and deceit, and tend to be modest and self-critical. A high or low level of Honesty-Humility reflects a person's moral principles and social interactions. People with high levels of Honesty-Humility generally inspire trust and respect from others because their behavior aligns with high ethical standards. Conversely, those who demonstrate low levels of this trait may be more prone to manipulation and dishonesty, which can negatively affect their reputation and relationships. ### Positive Aspects of High Honesty-Humility:. * **Trust from Others**: People with high Honesty-Humility usually inspire trust and respect, facilitating the creation of strong and long-lasting relationships. * **Ethical Behavior**: They make decisions based on moral principles, making them reliable partners in both personal and professional life. ### Negative Aspects of High Honesty-Humility:. * **Excessive Self-Criticism**: A high level of honesty can lead to excessive self-criticism and self-doubt. ### Positive Aspects of Low Honesty-Humility:. * **Ability to Achieve Goals**: People with low levels of Honesty-Humility may be more assertive and determined in achieving their goals. * **High Competitiveness**: A low level of honesty can allow them to be more aggressive in business and career, which can bring success. ### Negative Aspects of Low Honesty-Humility:. * **Unkind Behavior**: A tendency towards manipulation and deceit can lead to the destruction of trusting relationships and a negative reputation. * **Lack of Moral Principles**: People with low levels of this trait may make decisions that do not consider moral and ethical standards. * **Isolation from Others**: Low honesty and lack of humility can lead to alienation and distrust from others. ### Professions Suitable for People with High Levels of Honesty-Humility:. ### Professions Suitable for People with Low Levels of Honesty-Humility:. Honesty-Humility plays an important role in shaping personality and career choice.

results.title: The Case for More Intellectual Humility - Nautilus
results.content:
Title: The Case for More Intellectual Humility - Nautilus
It’s not easy changing someone’s mind, especially if what you’re trying to change is something like their settled opinion. If this amusing scene can be called anything, you might say that it’s a parody of intellectual humility or honesty. “If you think about what’s been wrong in Washington for a long time, it’s a whole lot of people who are very intellectually arrogant about the positions they have, on both sides of the aisle.”. Leary’s the author, along with some colleagues, of a new paper, titled “Cognitive and Interpersonal Features of Intellectual Humility.” The trait, they found, is “associated with variables related to openness, curiosity, tolerance of ambiguity, and low dogmatism.” Naturally, people high in intellectual humility expressed less certainty in their beliefs about religion and gave less weight to religious opinions in judging others; they also were less likely to deride politicians who change their positions as “flip-floppers.” What’s more, the researchers showed that people high in intellectual humility also were “more attuned to the strength of persuasive arguments than those who were low.” So intellectually humble people aren’t just humble because they’re bad at evaluating arguments. In a 2015 paper, a group of philosophers described intellectual humility as “proper attentiveness to, and owning, one’s intellectual limitations.” Would you say you’re intellectually humble? In response to *Edge*’s 2017 question, “What scientific term or concept ought to be more widely known?” he offered “intellectual honesty.” He thinks many of us find it hard attending to and owning our intellectual limitations. One way to cultivate more intellectual humility is to acknowledge how hard it is to really know something—especially when it comes to other people. How we might make a decision that’s mistaken or misguided in some way; how we might have a belief about the way the world works and it’s just not quite right…There’s nothing that we spend more time thinking about in our daily lives than other people. ## NAUTILUS: SCIENCE CONNECTED.
